findings.title: Do not skip installer validation when the Integration row is missing
findings.body: The Integration.DoesNotExist branch advances the pipeline before comparing the authenticated GitHub user with the installer. This can happen when the installation callback arrives before its webhook, or when webhook delivery fails. The subsequent build_integration call only fetches the installation using app credentials; it does not verify the authenticated user's relationship to it. Supplying another installation's ID in this state can therefore associate it with the current Sentry organization despite an installer mismatch. Apply the same validation on this path, or fail/retry until trusted installer metadata is available.

findings.title: Compare immutable GitHub user IDs instead of usernames
findings.body: The OAuth step stores the user's login, which GitHubInstallation compares with the webhook's sender.login snapshot. GitHub usernames can change, and old usernames can be claimed by other accounts. After an installer renames their account, the legitimate installer fails this check, while an unrelated account claiming the old name can pass it for an active, unlinked installation. Store and compare the immutable numeric user ID from the OAuth user response and webhook sender instead.

findings.title: Handle existing integrations without sender metadata
findings.body: An existing Integration is not guaranteed to contain sender metadata: build_integration only includes it when supplied in pipeline state, and the ordinary setup flow tested here produces metadata without it. If such an active Integration remains without an OrganizationIntegration, this new metadata['sender']['login'] access raises KeyError, turning a reconnect request into a server error. Missing sender data needs an explicit handled path that obtains trusted installer information or returns the installation-validation error.

findings.title: Keep the missing-installation test exercising the GitHub 404 path
findings.body: This test mocks the installation endpoint as returning 404 but now only asserts 'Invalid installation request.', which OAuth validation can return before that endpoint is reached. The production 404 handler is unchanged and still raises 'The GitHub installation could not be found.', so the replacement assertion allows an earlier callback rejection to satisfy the test without verifying its named behavior. Complete OAuth using the actual pipeline signature, verify that the installation endpoint was called, and retain the 404-specific error assertion.
